title: Matt Pocock on JSJ 538: why TypeScript beats JSDoc, inference, branded types and the safety-first mindset
summary: Matt Pocock defends TypeScript against panelists who prefer plain JavaScript with JSDoc. He covers refactor safety against changing back-end data contracts, TypeScript's inference strength, branded types, types-first design, and why generics mostly matter for library authors.

principles.text: TypeScript turns changing data contracts into compile errors, cutting bugs and runtime checking.
principles.quote: we would just get all these squiggly red lines wherever the data contract had changed and it meant that we didn't even have to test in the runtime anymore we knew that the types would be okay

principles.text: Adopting TypeScript can dramatically speed up a team by eliminating a whole class of bugs.
principles.quote: we put typescripts in and we immediately kind of almost doubled our velocity pretty much just by reducing a whole class of bugs

principles.text: You can adopt TypeScript gradually without embracing classes or inheritance; it doesn't force patterns on you.
principles.quote: you don't necessarily need to embrace classes or inheritance or anything like that

principles.text: TypeScript's real strength is deep inference and narrowing that understands JavaScript's own type system.
principles.quote: the thing that typescript is really really good at is inference

principles.text: Use branded types to stop mixing up values like different entity IDs at compile time.
principles.quote: I had different entity IDs mapped to different types and so you couldn't pass a user ID into something that was expecting a post ID

principles.text: Most app developers rarely need generics; complex type-level work is mainly for library authors.
principles.quote: most typescript users are not going to be dealing with generics really like maybe a couple of sort of basic stuff
